digest.top_line: Electron hypofractionation for BCC/SCC: 3-yr LRF 96.1% with 44 Gy/10 fx vs 97.5% with 54 Gy/18 fx, retrospective, 434 tumours.
digest.tldr: Skin RT carried the day, all retrospective or survey data with no randomised comparator. Short hypofractionated courses held LC (3-yr LRF 96.1% at 44 Gy/10 fx). For BCC 1.1-5 cm, ≤2 Gy/fx underperformed (LC 75%). Photon vs kV effects look confounded by indication. CNS: GK beat VMAT on plan quality only for mets ≤0.4 cc.

sites.intro: Four NMSC datasets on dose-fractionation and modality. Schedule and modality were assigned by era, frailty or lesion depth, so the comparisons stay confounded.

studies.name: UK practice survey: RT for non-melanoma skin cancer
studies.tldr: 63 UK clinical oncologists (43 complete) converge on 18-20 Gy/1#, 35 Gy/5#, 45 Gy/10#, 55 Gy/20#; 24 different non-standard schedules proposed.
details: 🔍 Anonymous online survey sent to 58 UK clinical heads/audit leads; open 3 months
🔍 43 complete + 20 partial responses; scenarios posed for a fit 65yo, well 80yo, frail 85yo
📊 Kilovoltage available to 81% of responders
📊 Workload: 46.2% treat <5 skin cases/month; only 2% treat skin exclusively

details.text: 📊 Most-suggested dose fractionations (Table 1, times suggested across scenarios)

details: 📊 Radical single fraction: 18 or 20 Gy in 94%; authors call 22 Gy/1# no longer acceptable unless correcting for stand-off

subdetails: Ala nasi 1.5-cm BCC: >80% kV photons, mostly 35 Gy/5#
Helix 2-cm SCC: kV used by only ~25%
Inner canthus BCC: ~80% kV; 74% apply stand-off correction (several at gap ≥5 mm)
Dorsum of hand 4-cm SCC: ~70% favour ≥15 fractions; 7.7% offered no regimen
Shin: ~20% decline RT even in the infirm
Graft recurrence: 40.6% treat whole graft, 50% recurrence + margin, 9.4% vary

details: ⚠️ BED modelling (α/β 3 for late effects) flags 28 Gy/2# 6 weeks apart, 32.4 Gy/3# weekly, 36 Gy/4# weekly as high late-effect risk
⚠️ Hypothetical scenario stems, no clinic gestalt; stated preference, not audited delivered practice
⚠️ 2014 survey, single country, 43 complete responses; no outcomes collected
studies.significance: The actionable read is in the weekly and alternate-day schedules for frail pts: BED modelling flags 28 Gy/2# 6 weeks apart, 32.4 Gy/3# weekly and 36 Gy/4# weekly as carrying excess late-effect risk. For single fractions, 18 or 20 Gy is the norm (94%); 22 Gy is called unacceptable without stand-off correction.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Anonymous Qualtrics survey of UK clinical oncologists treating NMSC, distributed via **58** clinical heads/audit leads, open 3 months. **43 complete and 20 partial** responses; median completion time 28 min.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Each scenario assumed tissue diagnosis and an MDT decision for **primary RT**, posed for a healthy 65yo, a relatively well 80yo and an 85yo nursing-home resident with early dementia and comorbidity.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Responses fell into single fraction, 3-5 fractions (27.5-35.0 Gy), 8-10 fractions (32-45 Gy), 15-33 fractions (45-66 Gy), and non-standard weekly/twice-weekly/alternate-day regimens. **Fitter pts got longer courses**; electrons were favoured for larger lesions and younger pts.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Four schedules dominated: **18-20 Gy/1#, 35 Gy/5#, 45 Gy/10#, 55 Gy/20#**. Non-standard fractionation was highly heterogeneous, with **24 different schedules** proposed.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: No randomised data exist to compare against; the authors benchmark responses against retrospective series, e.g. 30 Gy/5# over 4 weeks giving 95.2% local control in 42 BCCs and kV over nasal cartilage giving good/acceptable cosmesis in 96.8%. Daily schedules matched published international practice.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents UK clinical-oncologist preference for primary RT of BCC/cSCC across head-and-neck, hand, shin and graft scenarios. Does not represent outcomes, adjuvant/nodal RT, or current (post-2014) practice.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Partial completers gave under 1 min, so the denominator is effectively 43. Kilovoltage access (81%) shaped modality answers, conflating preference with availability.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Daily schedules are largely settled; the real variance sits in **non-standard regimens for frail pts** and **graft recurrences** (near-even split on whole-graft vs margin). Authors argue for centres publishing local outcomes to harmonise practice.

studies.interpretation:
The value of this survey is less in its headline, that UK skin RT clusters around four daily schedules, than in where it shows that consensus breaking down. For a fit patient with a standard head-and-neck lesion, the answers line up with the retrospective literature the authors cite, and there is little here to move a practising radiation oncologist. The spread opens up in exactly the patients where evidence is thinnest: the frail elderly patient who cannot attend daily, the lesion over cartilage, the shin or dorsum of the hand where wound healing is poor, and recurrence inside a graft.

The weekly and alternate-day regimens are the most clinically useful section. Respondents proposed 24 different non-standard schedules, and the authors' linear-quadratic comparison suggests the three most common (45 Gy/9# over 3 weeks, 27 Gy/3# over 2 weeks, and a 38 Gy/6# schedule) behave similarly for tumour, while several others (28 Gy/2# six weeks apart, 32.4 Gy/3# weekly, 36 Gy/4# weekly) carry a late-effect BED that should give pause if the patient lives long enough to show it. That argument rests on modelled parameters (α/β 8.5 Gy for tumour, 3 Gy for late effects) rather than observed outcomes, so it identifies schedules to scrutinise, not schedules proven harmful. There is also an internal inconsistency worth noticing: the 38 Gy/6# regimen is listed as over 6 weeks in Table 1 and over 3 weeks in the BED discussion, which matters for any time-corrected calculation.

The cartilage findings show practice diverging from the authors' own reading of the data. Over 80% would use kilovoltage for a small ala nasi BCC, yet only about a quarter would for a helical SCC, despite retrospective series supporting kilovoltage at the ear. The authors attribute this to local experience of complications and speculate on a vascular contribution at the pinna; that is plausible but untested, and the scenario mixed histology (BCC nose, SCC ear), which muddies the comparison.

Methodologically, this is stated preference on hypothetical stems, with 43 complete responses and no outcome data, from 2014. Respondents with limited skin workload (nearly half see under five cases a month) are included alongside high-volume clinicians, and modality answers are partly a proxy for kilovoltage availability. The result should be read as a reference map of acceptable UK schedules and a flag on a handful of weekly regimens, not as evidence that any schedule is superior.

What it does not settle is the question it repeatedly raises: which non-standard regimen gives durable control with tolerable late effects in frail patients, and whether the whole graft needs treating. Both remain open, and neither can be answered by surveys.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: The actionable read is in the weekly and alternate-day schedules for frail pts: BED modelling flags 28 Gy/2# 6 weeks apart, 32.4 Gy/3# weekly and 36 Gy/4# weekly as carrying excess late-effect risk. For single fractions, 18 or 20 Gy is the norm (94%); 22 Gy is called unacceptable without stand-off correction.

open_questions: Optimal non-standard fractionation for frail elderly NMSC pts
Whole graft vs recurrence-plus-margin for recurrence within skin graft
Kilovoltage safety over ear cartilage vs nasal cartilage

studies.name: Radiotherapy for epithelial skin cancer
studies.tldr: Overall local control 89% across 531 lesions; 93% untreated vs 80% recurrent, with fraction size, diameter and histology independently predicting local failure.
details: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective review, 1966-1997, 468 pts with 531 biopsy-proven lesions
🔍 389 BCC and 142 SCC; 167 lesions were recurrent at presentation
🔍 Median f/u 5.8 yr (range 2-24); minimum 2 yr follow-up

subdetails: Superficial x-rays 60%
Electron beam 19%
Electron + superficial combination 20%
Megavoltage photons <2%

details.text: 📊 Local tumor control by histology and presentation
📊 Local control by modality, all lesions

details: 📐 Modality not significant on multivariate analysis (electrons vs other, p=0.345)

details.text: 📊 BCC 1.1-5 cm: local control by dose per fraction (p=0.01, ≤2 Gy vs larger)

details: 📐 Multivariate: larger fraction size associated with better LC (p=0.01); diameter and histology p<0.01
📊 SCC: no clear dose-response or fraction-size effect (≤1 cm lesions p=0.13)
📊 SCC T4: LC 75% (9 of 12) with cartilage invasion, 67% (14 of 21) with bone invasion
📊 SCC nodal involvement 13% overall; 32% in recurrent lesions

subdetails: 92% excellent/good cosmesis among pts with cosmesis data
Overall complication rate 5.8%; 13% in lesions >5 cm
Soft-tissue necrosis: 13 (9%) of 142 SCC vs 8 (2%) of 389 BCC
Fair/poor cosmesis: superficial 12 (4%) of 276, electrons 10 (12%) of 81, combination 15 (19%) of 77

details: ⚠️ Modality assigned by era and lesion features, not randomized; superficial arm skewed to small lesions
⚠️ Cosmesis scored retrospectively from notes and photographs; data missing for 15-25% of untreated lesions
🔗 Same institution's 1986 Lovett series found electrons worse on multivariate; authors attribute the change to larger electron margins in recent years

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective series spanning three decades; modality and fractionation were not randomized and track lesion size and era, so modality and fraction-size comparisons are confounded.
verdict.audience: BCC or SCC of the skin, untreated or recurrent, definitive RT

studies.significance: The actionable RT signal is fraction size: BCC 1.1-5 cm treated at ≤2 Gy/fx controlled 75% (38/51) vs 95-100% with larger fractions (p=0.01), and fraction size held on multivariate analysis. That argues against conventional 2 Gy fractionation for mid-size BCC, while SCC showed no comparable dose or fraction-size effect.
studies.monday_clinic: In mid-size (1.1-5 cm) BCC treated with definitive RT, this supports hypofractionated over ≤2 Gy/fx schedules; it does not establish a fractionation preference for SCC, where no dose-response was seen.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Retrospective single-institution review of consecutive pts treated **1966 to 1997**. **468 pts, 531 lesions**; median follow-up **5.8 yr** (range 2-24).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Biopsy-proven epithelial skin cancer: **389 BCC, 142 SCC**; **167 recurrent** lesions. Median age 73 (BCC) and 72 (SCC); AJCC staging.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: **Superficial x-rays 60%**, electrons 19%, electron + superficial combination 20%, megavoltage photons <2%. Treatment area was tumor plus microscopic extension with an additional **1 cm margin** depending on size; lead eye shields used near the orbit.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Local tumor control (relapse-free from RT start), cosmesis graded by telangiectasia, pigmentation and fibrosis, and complications.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: Overall LC **89%**. Multivariate predictors of local failure: **daily fraction size (p=0.01)**, maximal diameter and histology (p<0.01); modality, age and treatment duration were not significant.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Complication rate **5.8%** (13% in lesions >5 cm), mostly soft-tissue necrosis: **9% of SCC vs 2% of BCC**. Fair/poor cosmesis was more frequent with combination (19%) and electron (12%) treatment than superficial (4%).

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Consistent with Silva et al., who also found tumor size and low dose per fraction predicted local failure in pinna lesions. Departs from the same institution's 1986 Lovett series, where electrons were associated with worse LC on multivariate analysis.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents BCC and cSCC treated with definitive orthovoltage or electron RT, including recurrent lesions. Does not represent modern image-guided, HDR surface brachytherapy, or adjuvant post-Mohs settings.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: A three-decade span crosses changes in electron technique, bolus policy and margins. Megavoltage photon cohort (n=6) is too small to interpret. SCC fraction-size tables are sparse per cell.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: RT delivers high LC for small untreated lesions regardless of histology, with **96-100%** for lesions ≤1 cm. Recurrence at presentation and larger diameter cost the most control, and fraction size is the one dose parameter the data suggest is modifiable for BCC.

studies.interpretation:
This series is best read as a long-horizon institutional audit rather than a comparative study. It shows a well-known pattern for skin cancer RT: small, previously untreated lesions are controlled almost uniformly, and the room for error opens up with size, recurrence and squamous histology. Its value to a contemporary radiation oncologist is less the headline 89% local control, which is consistent with what most departments would expect, than the specific parameters it ties to failure.

The most actionable of these is fraction size. In basal cell lesions of 1.1 to 5 cm, schedules at 2 Gy or less per fraction controlled 75% of lesions while larger fractions controlled 95% to 100%, and fraction size held up on multivariate analysis at p=0.01. That supports the hypofractionated schedules many departments already favor for BCC, and it pushes back on conventional fractionation as a default for mid-size lesions on the theory that it is gentler. The caution is that fraction size here was not assigned at random. Physicians over thirty years chose schedules for reasons that may track anatomy, lesion depth, patient frailty or era, and the ≤2 Gy cells are small enough that a handful of failures moves the percentage considerably. The squamous data show no such signal, but the per-cell counts are even thinner, so absence of effect there is not evidence of equivalence.

The modality comparison needs the most care. Superficial x-rays look clearly better in raw local control, yet modality fell out on multivariate analysis, which is what one would expect if superficial treatment was simply reserved for smaller, more favorable lesions. The authors' own explanation for why electrons no longer underperformed compared with their 1986 report, namely wider margins in later years, is itself a technique argument: electron failures are plausibly a problem of penumbra and margin, not of the particle. The cosmesis gradient favoring superficial treatment carries the same confounding, since larger lesions received electrons or combinations and larger lesions had worse cosmesis regardless.

The recurrence data are the cleanest clinical message. Recurrent squamous lesions controlled at 68% against 89% when untreated, and nodal involvement in recurrent squamous disease reached 32%. Whatever modality is chosen first, an inadequate initial treatment appears to cost more than any downstream choice can recover, which matters in multidisciplinary discussions about marginal excisions or destructive treatments for higher-risk lesions.

What this series cannot settle is how RT compares with Mohs surgery or excision for the same lesion, how modern techniques such as surface brachytherapy or image-guided electrons would perform, or whether the BCC fraction-size effect survives adjustment for the selection that produced it. For those questions it offers hypotheses and a consistent historical baseline, not answers.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Fraction size, not modality, carried the multivariate signal: BCC 1.1-5 cm at ≤2 Gy/fx controlled 75% (38/51) vs 95-100% with larger fractions (p=0.01). Electron LC gaps narrowed once margins widened, so electron technique and margin matter more than beam choice itself.
significance_by_specialty.surgonc: Recurrent lesions, a third of which had failed surgery, electrodessication or prior RT elsewhere, controlled at 80% vs 93% untreated, and SCC nodal involvement reached 32% in recurrent disease. The cost of an inadequate first treatment is the read for anyone choosing initial local therapy.

open_questions: Does the BCC fraction-size effect survive in prospective or modern-technique cohorts?
RT vs Mohs surgery for recurrent cutaneous SCC
Optimal electron margin for SCC to match superficial x-ray control

studies.name: Hypofractionated electron beam RT for epithelial skin cancer (434 cases)
studies.tldr: 3-yr local recurrence-free rate 97.5% with 54 Gy/18 fx vs 96.1% with 44 Gy/10 fx, using electrons for BCC and SCC in a retrospective series.
details: 🔍 Single-centre retrospective series: 434 biopsy-proven tumours in 333 pts, treated 2001-2006
🔍 54 Gy/18 fx of 3 Gy (n=159) vs 44 Gy/10 fx of 4.4 Gy (n=275), 4 fx per week

details.text: 📊 3-yr actuarial local recurrence-free (LRF) rate by histology and schedule

details: 📊 T stage was the only significant factor for local recurrence (p=0.036)
📊 2 of 11 T3 (>5 cm) tumours recurred, both after 44 Gy; centre now gives 54 Gy for >5 cm
📊 15 local recurrences in total; median time to recurrence 10.4 mo for BCC, 3.3 mo for SCC
📊 3-yr MFS 98.8% overall; all 5 metastatic events in SCC (3-yr MFS 94.7%)
📊 3-yr OS 54% SCC vs 82% BCC; most deaths from other causes, 3-yr CSS 98% and 100%

details.text: 📊 Cosmesis pilot (14 pts), good or fair outcome

details: ⚠️ Schedule assigned by era and frailty: 44 Gy cohort older (>80 y: 41.2% vs 17.0%)
⚠️ Follow-up shorter in the 44 Gy group, as the authors acknowledge
⚠️ BCC 44 Gy 3-yr LRF is 96.9% in the text but 96.7% in the Fig 1 caption

verdict.rationale: Single-centre retrospective series. Schedule was assigned by era and frailty, not randomised, and follow-up was unequal. It cannot establish equivalence of the two fractionations.
verdict.audience: Elderly pts, biopsy-proven BCC/SCC, mostly face/head, primary or postop

studies.significance: Technique details decide whether this transfers: electron energy 4-12 MeV chosen by estimated depth, a 1 cm margin, and copper foil (0.2 or 0.4 mm) to offset electron skin sparing. SCC has the thinnest evidence: only 33 tumours got 54 Gy, with a 3-yr LRF 95% CI of 79.1-99.6%. The 10-fraction course is better supported for BCC than for SCC.
studies.monday_clinic: For an elderly pt with T1-T2 BCC or SCC, this supports a 10-fraction electron course on local control. It does not cover tumours >5 cm: both T3 local failures followed 44 Gy, and the authors' own centre has gone back to 54 Gy for these.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: **Single-centre retrospective** analysis of 434 tumours in 333 pts treated 2001-2006. Analysed **per tumour**; a pt could contribute several lesions, and no correction was made for this.

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: Biopsy-proven epithelial skin cancer: **332 BCC and 102 SCC**. Treatment was primary after biopsy (n=386) or postop for residual disease (n=48). Median age was 74.8 y for BCC and 78.3 y for SCC, and most tumours were on the face (59.4%) or elsewhere on the head (22.4%).

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Electrons, **54 Gy/18 fx of 3 Gy** or **44 Gy/10 fx of 4.4 Gy**, given 4 times per week. Energy 4-12 MeV by estimated tumour depth, target was the tumour plus a **1 cm margin**, and copper foil compensated for skin sparing. From January 2004, 44 Gy became the standard.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: LRF and metastasis-free rates were calculated as one minus cumulative incidence, with death as a competing risk. OS and CSS used Kaplan-Meier. Too few events allowed only univariate log-rank analysis of prognostic factors.

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: The histology-by-schedule LRF figures are in the table. The one significant risk factor was **T stage (p=0.036)**, carried by 2 of 11 T3 tumours recurring after 44 Gy.

analysis_sections.label: Safety
analysis_sections.body: Cosmesis was scored only in a **14-pt pilot**: good or fair in 75% vs 100% (patient-scored) and 87% vs 83% (observer-scored) for 54 vs 44 Gy, with no significant difference. 'Poor' scores did not track fractionation, site, size or location.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The authors place their LRF at or above the prior RT series they cite, which reported **87-97% for BCC and 56-91% for SCC**, and as comparable to surgical series. Some earlier reports found electrons inferior to superficial X-rays, which the authors attribute to inadequate margins or uncompensated skin sparing.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents elderly pts with T1-T2 BCC or SCC, mostly on the face or head, treated with electrons using a 1 cm margin and surface compensation. Does not represent tumours >5 cm, younger pts, or kilovoltage or brachytherapy techniques.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The 44 Gy cohort was **much older** (>80 y: 41.2% vs 17.0%), so competing mortality may hide late recurrences. Cosmesis photos were taken at a median of 66 vs 22 mo, so late effects of 4.4 Gy fractions are not captured. T stage was missing for some tumours, and the text and Fig 1 disagree on one LRF value.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Both schedules gave LRF in the mid to high 90s at 3 y. The authors argue that most BCC and SCC recurrences occur early, which partly offsets the shorter follow-up. What remains open is whether 4.4 Gy fractions match 3 Gy fractions for late cosmesis, and whether 44 Gy is enough for large tumours.

studies.interpretation:
The core claim is that a 10-fraction electron course gives the same local control as an 18-fraction course for BCC and SCC. Read carefully, that claim is plausible but not demonstrated. This is a comparison across eras with confounding by indication. The shorter schedule was first offered to elderly, less mobile pts and only became the default in 2004. The 44 Gy group is therefore older, has shorter follow-up, and dies sooner of other causes. Each of those pushes observed recurrence downward in the hypofractionated arm. Competing-risk methodology handles death correctly as an event, but it cannot recover recurrences in pts who died before they would have recurred. Equivalent 3-yr LRF in this setting is a weaker statement than it looks.

The authors' main defence is the timing of recurrence. BCC failures came at a median of 10.4 mo and SCC failures at 3.3 mo, so most events should fall inside the observed window. That argument is reasonable for SCC. It is less convincing for BCC: the recurrence range ran to 65 mo, and only 90% of BCC failures occurred within 3 y. A late BCC tail in the older cohort is exactly what this design would miss.

The most useful signal is the T stage gradient. T stage was the only significant prognostic factor, and both T3 failures followed 44 Gy. With 11 T3 tumours, this is fragile. Still, it fits a radiobiological intuition that a short course with a larger fraction size may lose margin on bulky disease. The authors acted on it by returning tumours >5 cm to 54 Gy. Their final recommendation is deliberately limited to T1-T2 disease, and readers should hold to that boundary.

SCC carries less certainty than BCC. The SCC confidence intervals are wide, especially in the 54 Gy group, and all metastatic events were in SCC. A non-significant p-value in groups this small is absence of evidence rather than evidence of equivalence. The finding transfers more confidently to BCC.

Technique also limits transfer. The results depend on a 1 cm margin, energy matched to estimated depth, and copper-foil compensation for skin sparing. The authors explicitly link earlier inferior electron results to inadequate margins and uncompensated skin sparing. A reader using kilovoltage beams, smaller margins, or different bolus practice is extrapolating. Cosmesis is the weakest arm of the argument: 14 pts, photographed at very different intervals, cannot speak to late effects of 4.4 Gy fractions.

On balance, the paper supports what many departments already do: a short electron course for frail, elderly pts with small facial BCC, where travel burden matters and life expectancy limits late-effect exposure. It does not settle fractionation for large tumours, for SCC with high-risk features, or for younger pts, in whom late cosmesis and late recurrence dominate the decision.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: For T1-T2 BCC and SCC, 44 Gy/10 fx of 4.4 Gy matched 54 Gy/18 fx on 3-yr LRF, given with a 1 cm margin and copper-foil compensation. Both T3 failures followed 44 Gy, so the 10-fraction course is best kept to tumours up to 5 cm. Support is stronger for BCC than SCC.

open_questions: Is 44 Gy in 10 fractions adequate for tumours over 5 cm?
Late cosmesis after 4.4 Gy fractions beyond two years
Does the short course hold for high-risk SCC?

⚠️ Logistic regression on crude recurrence with median f/u 18.4mo (range 0-132); censoring not modelled
⚠️ Per-tumour analysis with no correction for multiple lesions per pt
🔗 vs van Hezewijk 44/10 vs 54/18: 3-yr LC 96.1% vs 96.9%, higher-EQD2 schedules than here

verdict.rationale: Single-centre predictor analysis using logistic regression without time-to-event censoring; modality effect confounded by lesion depth and size selection.
verdict.audience: BCC/SCC skin, RT primary, salvage or postop, median age 78

studies.significance: Dose did not track with control here (EQD2 OR 1.007, p=0.4735), yet LC was 84.2% on schedules of EQD2 56 and 47, below the 96.1% and 96.9% van Hezewijk reported with 44/10 and 54/18. That gap, plus photons used for deeper lesions, leaves the dose question for ≥2cm or immunosuppressed lesions unanswered rather than settled.
studies.monday_clinic: In an elderly or immunosuppressed pt with a BCC or SCC ≥2cm treated with RT, this flags roughly two- to threefold higher odds of local recurrence; it does not show that orthovoltage or electrons outperform photons for a lesion of equal depth.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-centre cohort from a **prospective NMSC clinic database**, RT delivered Jan 2007 to Dec 2011. Analysis per tumour; **univariate then backwards logistic regression** (UVA p<0.10 entered).

analysis_sections.label: Population & inclusion
analysis_sections.body: 389 pts, **448 lesions**, median age 78. BCC 46.2%, sclerosing BCC 25.7%, SCC 28.1%; primary 53.3%, recurrent 29.7%, postoperative 16.7%; **9% of lesions in immunosuppressed pts**.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Most common **50 Gy/20 fx** (26.3%) and **40 Gy/10 fx** (14.5%). Orthovoltage 41.1%, electrons 32.6%, photons 26.3%; electrons or photons for tumours >1cm thick or >3cm, 1-2cm margin to field edge.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: Clinically assessed local recurrence, calculated from the last RT day. Follow-up to discharge at 2y (BCC) or 3y (sclerosing BCC, SCC).

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: **LC 84.2%** at median follow-up 18.4mo; median time to recurrence 11.4mo. Multivariate predictors are tabulated above.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: Prior series cited by the authors report LC of 87%-98% for primary BCC and 56%-97% for SCC. The van Hezewijk series reached **3-yr LC 96.1% and 96.9%** with 44/10 and 54/18 (EQD2 63 and 70), vs EQD2 56 and 47 for the schedules used here.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents older pts with BCC or SCC treated with orthovoltage, electron or photon RT in primary, recurrent or postoperative settings. Does not represent melanoma, nodal disease, or a randomized comparison of modality or dose.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: Range of follow-up starts at 0 months, so lesions with short follow-up count as controlled. No correction for multiple tumours per pt, and immunosuppression covers only 39 lesions, which accounts for the wide CI (1.321-6.539).

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: Size and immunosuppression agree with earlier series; age as a predictor conflicts with most prior work. The photon penalty most likely reflects deeper, larger lesions, **not inferior beam quality**, and lack of a dose signal may reflect a narrow dose range.

studies.interpretation:
The useful part of this series is not the list of predictors, most of which a skin radiation oncologist would already have named, but what it says about how much the familiar risk factors shift outcomes in an unselected, elderly clinic population. Lesion size of 2cm or more and host immunosuppression each carried roughly two- to threefold odds of recurrence after adjustment, and both agree with the earlier literature the authors cite. Age is the outlier: the authors acknowledge most prior work finds it irrelevant, and a per-year OR of 1.034 in a cohort with a median age of 78 is a small effect that may be capturing competing risk, frailty-driven dose choices, or follow-up patterns rather than tumour biology.

The modality result needs the most caution. Orthovoltage and electrons both look protective against photons, but the protocol itself assigned electrons or photons to tumours thicker than 1cm or larger than 3cm, and the authors say photons were reserved for deeper, more extensive lesions. Size was dichotomised at 2cm and depth was not modelled at all, so the regression cannot separate beam from lesion. A reader should not take this as evidence that photons are an inferior treatment for a lesion that could equally be treated with orthovoltage; it is evidence that the lesions sent to photons were worse. The authors also note that earlier series showing poorer results with electrons than orthovoltage may reflect field size and technique, which reinforces that modality comparisons in nonrandomised skin series largely track selection and planning quality.

The dose finding is the one most likely to be misread. EQD2 showed no association with recurrence, but the two dominant schedules, 40 Gy in 10 and 50 Gy in 20, sit at EQD2 56 and 47 by the authors' calculation, a narrow band. Absence of a dose-response inside that band says little about whether moving toward the higher EQD2 schedules in the van Hezewijk series, which reported 3-year control above 96%, would close the gap to this cohort's 84.2%. The overall control rate here is lower than several comparison series, and the authors do not resolve whether that reflects case mix (nearly a third of lesions were recurrent, a sixth postoperative), dose, or methodology.

Methodology is the main reason to hold these estimates loosely. Recurrence was analysed by logistic regression on a crude rate, not as time to event, with follow-up ranging from zero months and a median of 18.4. Lesions with brief follow-up enter as controlled, which biases control upward and can distort predictor estimates if follow-up differs by group. Analysis was per tumour with no adjustment for clustering within pts, and the immunosuppressed group is only 39 lesions, reflected in a confidence interval running from about 1.3 to 6.5. The recurrent-versus-primary comparison trended toward higher risk without reaching significance, which in a sample this size is a power problem, not reassurance.

What would make the main conclusions wrong? If immunosuppressed or large-lesion pts were systematically followed longer, their apparent excess risk would partly be a detection artefact. The direction of the size and immunosuppression signals is consistent enough with prior series that this seems unlikely to reverse them, but the magnitudes should not be quoted as calibrated risk estimates. The decision this series supports is closer surveillance and careful technique in large or immunosuppressed lesions; it does not support choosing a modality or a dose schedule.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Dose did not track with control (EQD2 OR 1.007, p=0.4735), but the two dominant schedules spanned only EQD2 56 and 47, and LC was 84.2% vs the 96.1% and 96.9% reported with 44/10 and 54/18. For ≥2cm or immunosuppressed lesions, the schedule question stays open; the photon penalty reflects depth selection, not beam choice.

open_questions: Would higher-EQD2 schedules improve control in lesions ≥2cm?
Does the photon penalty persist after adjusting for lesion depth?
Optimal RT approach for NMSC in immunosuppressed pts

sites.intro: Dosimetry-only planning study with no local control or radionecrosis endpoint.

studies.name: Volume threshold of brain metastases for Linac-based SRS
studies.tldr: GK beat VMAT plan quality for brain mets ≤0.4 cc. Above 0.4 cc, SmartArc and HyperArc beat GK on RTOG CI and NT V12Gy, with ~8-14 vs 56 min beam-on.
details: 🔍 Single-institution retrospective planning study: 26 pts, 2-3 brain mets each, 76 lesions
🔍 GK SRS pts from 2018-2019, replanned as SmartArc (Pinnacle) and HyperArc (Eclipse) VMAT
🔍 Linac plans used HD-120 MLC + FFF beams; median 3 targets per pt
📐 ROC on RTOG CI + NT V12Gy (GK as baseline) set each technique's threshold volume

details.text: 📊 Median plan metrics, targets ≤0.4 cc (GK vs VMAT)
📊 Median plan metrics, targets >0.4 cc (GK vs VMAT)

details: 📊 Median beam-on: GK 56.25 min vs SmartArc 8.33 vs HyperArc 13.58, both p<0.0001 vs GK
⚠️ The 0.4 cc cutoff is an average of four ROC thresholds (0.4, 0.2, 0.4, 0.5 cc), not a single prespecified analysis
⚠️ HyperArc CI threshold PPV only 35.0%. The 0.2 cc cutoff is weakly predictive.
⚠️ Dosimetry only: no local control, radionecrosis or clinical endpoint reported
🔗 Consistent with Potrebko (1.16 cc mean-volume split) and Vergalasova (>1 cm diameter) direction. Different binning limits direct comparison.

verdict.rationale: Single-institution retrospective replanning of 26 pts with dosimetric endpoints only; threshold averaged across ad hoc ROC cutoffs, no clinical outcome validation.
verdict.audience: 2-3 brain mets, SRS candidates, GK vs linac VMAT platform choice

studies.significance: Platform choice depends on the smallest lesion. For targets ≤0.4 cc, GK beat SmartArc on every metric, while HyperArc matched GK on NT V12Gy (0.7 vs 0.79 cc, p=0.1923) but had higher low-dose spill. Above 0.4 cc, both VMAT techniques gave lower CI and V12Gy in roughly a quarter of the beam-on time.
studies.monday_clinic: In a pt with 2-3 brain mets all above 0.4 cc, this supports single-isocenter VMAT SRS as dosimetrically at least equivalent to GK; it does not extend to sub-0.4 cc lesions or to pts with more than 4 mets.

analysis_sections.label: Design
analysis_sections.body: Single-institution **retrospective treatment-planning comparison**. 121 GK pts with 2-3 targets were screened (2018-2019) and **26 pts / 76 lesions** were selected and replanned with SmartArc and HyperArc VMAT.

analysis_sections.label: Radiotherapy
analysis_sections.body: Linac plans used **HD-120 MLC with FFF beams**, with two isocenters in the illustrated cases. Example prescriptions were 13 Gy and 24 Gy. Mean target coverage was 100% GK, 99.62% SmartArc and 99.73% HyperArc.

analysis_sections.label: Endpoints
analysis_sections.body: RTOG CI, Paddick GI, NT V12Gy and V4.5Gy. ROC analysis on **RTOG CI and NT V12Gy** set the threshold volume below which GK wins. Lesions whose isodoses couldn't be separated were excluded (71 targets for CI, 60 for V12Gy).

analysis_sections.label: Results
analysis_sections.body: SmartArc thresholds were **0.4 cc** for both CI and V12Gy. HyperArc thresholds were **0.2 cc (CI) and 0.5 cc (V12Gy)**. The authors propose **0.4 cc** as a single VMAT SRS threshold.

analysis_sections.label: vs leading data
analysis_sections.body: The direction agrees with Potrebko (GK lower V12Gy below a 1.16 cc mean-volume split) and Vergalasova (VMAT more conformal above a 1 cm diameter, about 0.52 cc). Those studies had a median of 8 and 7 targets per pt, against 3 here. Kim et al. used 5-mm MLC without FFF in vestibular schwannoma.

analysis_sections.label: Applies to
analysis_sections.body: Represents linac SRS planning for pts with 2-3 brain mets on modern HD MLC/FFF platforms. Does not represent pts with more than 4 mets, older 5-mm MLC linacs, or any clinical outcome endpoint.

analysis_sections.label: Limitations
analysis_sections.body: The single 0.4 cc cutoff averages four technique- and metric-specific ROC thresholds. HyperArc's CI threshold had a PPV of 35.0%. Excluding closely adjacent targets removes the cases where MLC dose bridging matters most.

analysis_sections.label: Discussion
analysis_sections.body: For lesions ≤0.4 cc, HyperArc narrows the GK gap on conformity and V12Gy but not on low-dose spread. The open question is whether V4.5Gy differences of a few cc matter clinically when there are only 2-3 targets.

studies.interpretation:
The question this paper asks is practical: when a department has both a Gamma Knife and a modern linac, which lesions should go where? Its answer is a volume cutoff of 0.4 cc. GK's small collimators and sharp penumbra win below it, and VMAT-based SRS wins above it on conformity and V12Gy, with far shorter beam-on time. For a radiation oncologist, the useful takeaway is narrower than the headline. Most brain mets treated with SRS are larger than 0.4 cc, so for the typical 2-3 lesion case on a modern HD-MLC FFF linac, this supports the view that the linac is not dosimetrically second best.

How the cutoff was derived should temper confidence in the exact number. The four ROC analyses produced thresholds of 0.4, 0.2, 0.4 and 0.5 cc, and the authors averaged them into one figure. That is a pragmatic simplification, not a validated decision rule. The HyperArc thresholds diverge by metric, and the HyperArc conformity threshold had a positive predictive value of only 35.0%. The HyperArc data also suggest the platform-dependent answer is shifting. Below 0.4 cc, HyperArc did not lose to GK on NT V12Gy (0.7 vs 0.79 cc, p=0.1923) and had lower median RTOG CI. Its remaining deficit was low-dose spread (V4.5Gy and GI). So the honest version of the finding is that GK holds a small-target low-dose advantage over HyperArc, and a broader small-target advantage over SmartArc.

Against prior work, the direction is consistent. Potrebko found GK sparing V12Gy better below a 1.16 cc mean-volume split, and Vergalasova found VMAT more conformal above a 1 cm diameter. This study's threshold is lower than both. The authors attribute that to the HD-120 MLC and FFF beams, and to fewer targets per pt (median 3, vs 8 and 7 in those series). MLC leakage and dose bridging between targets grow with lesion count, so the 0.4 cc cutoff should not be carried over to a 6-10 lesion case. The exclusion of closely adjacent targets whose isodoses could not be separated also removes exactly the geometry where linac dose bridging would hurt most.

For this result to be wrong in practice, either dosimetric surrogates would need to fail to predict radionecrosis and local control, or the selected 26 pts would need to be unrepresentative. Neither is tested here. V12Gy is a reasonable radionecrosis surrogate, but absolute differences of tenths of a cc for sub-0.4 cc lesions are unlikely to move clinical risk by themselves. The practical use of the paper is as a triage heuristic for a dual-platform department: send the case to the linac when every lesion is comfortably above the cutoff, and weigh GK when the smallest lesion is tiny and low-dose spill matters. It does not settle whether any of this changes outcomes.

significance_by_specialty.radonc: Platform choice depends on the smallest lesion. For targets ≤0.4 cc, GK beat SmartArc on every metric, while HyperArc matched GK on NT V12Gy but had higher low-dose spill. Above 0.4 cc, both VMAT techniques gave lower CI and V12Gy with median beam-on of 8.33 and 13.58 vs 56.25 min.

open_questions: Does the 0.4 cc threshold hold for more than 4 brain mets?
Do V12Gy differences translate into radionecrosis or local control differences?
Does HyperArc close the small-target low-dose gap with GK?

Predictors of Recurrence after Radiotherapy for Non-Melanoma Skin Cancer
papers.abstract: Predictive factors of recurrence were examined in 448 non-melanoma skin cancers (72% basal cell carcinoma, 28% squamous cell carcinoma) treated with radiotherapy. The overall recurrence rate was 15.8% at a median follow-up of 18.4 months. In multivariate analysis, significant factors for recurrence were age (p = 0.0197), tumour size 2 cm or greater (p = 0.0095), immunosuppression (p = 0.0082), and treatment modality (p = 0.0009).
